atlas.blurb: Anne Dacier's learned 1716 prose Odyssey became the standard French Homer of the eighteenth century. She published it amid the Quarrel of the Ancients and Moderns, defending ancient poetry against Houdar de la Motte's streamlined Homer in a public argument over taste, fidelity, and progress. Pope found her scholarship useful for his own translations, even as their judgments diverged and Dacier later objected to his liberties.

peers.name: Leconte de Lisle
peers.atlasBlurb: Leconte de Lisle's 1867 prose Odyssey re-Greeked French. It rejected three centuries of Latinized convention—no Ulysse, no Minerve—and restored Odysseus, Troiè, and Ithakè in slow, hieratic prose meant to sound ancient rather than polite. Its austere vocabulary, antique names, and sculpted cadence made it a durable literary standard and a counterweight to smoother classroom prose for generations of French readers.

atlas.blurb: Shaul Tchernichovsky's 1940 Dvir Odyssey was the first complete Hebrew translation, carrying all twenty-four books into dactylic hexameter. Later Schocken and Am Oved editions kept this landmark Hebrew Homer in print and online.

peers.name: Voß
peers.atlasBlurb: Johann Heinrich Voß's 1781 Odüssee is the German Homer: a philologically exacting version in strict dactylic hexameters that 'made the poem national with the Germans.' Voß revised it for four decades, but the fresher 1781 text is often preferred. It fixed the classical hexameter in German ears and became the measure every later German Homer had to accept or refuse, including Schadewaldt's prose.

peers.name: Cotterill
peers.atlasBlurb: A complete Odyssey in English hexameters, published in Boston in 1911: 'Sing, O Muse, of the man so wary and wise.' Cotterill's rolling six-beat lines are one of the era's most sustained attempts to echo Homer's own metre.

peers.name: Zhukovsky
peers.atlasBlurb: Russia's canonical Odyssey — made by a translator who barely read Greek. Zhukovsky, elder statesman of Russian Romantic poetry, worked in 1842–44 and 1848–49 from a word-by-word German interlinear prepared at his request by the Düsseldorf philologist Karl Grashof, with each Greek word's grammar spelled out beneath it. Out of that scaffolding he built flowing Russian hexameters that contemporaries hailed as a resurrection of Homer, and that remained the Russian Odyssey for over a century.

peers.name: Vosmaer
peers.atlasBlurb: The Hague man of letters Carel Vosmaer finished his Dutch hexameter Odussee just before his death; published in 1889, it paired with his 1880 Ilias to reign for decades as the classic Dutch Homer.

peers.name: Wilster
peers.atlasBlurb: Denmark's first complete Odyssey, in hexameters blending archaism, colloquial ease, and Romantic color; for generations Wilster's twin Homer versions simply signaled Homer to Danish readers, reprinted from Reitzel to Museum Tusculanum.

atlas.blurb: After Leviathan and the civil wars, Thomas Hobbes spent his final decade on Homer, publishing a complete Odyssey in 1675 as 'the amusement of his old age.' The verse is plain, brisk, and story-first. Pope praised its general sense but faulted its omissions, then judged Hobbes's poetry, 'as well as Ogilby's,' too mean for criticism. Three editions appeared within little more than a decade.

peers.name: Murray
peers.atlasBlurb: A. T. Murray's Odyssey filled the Loeb Classical Library's Homer shelves from 1919: Greek on the left-hand page, 'a fairly literal translation' facing it, exactly as the series' brief required. His careful, slightly formal prose — 'Tell me, O Muse, of the man of many devices' — became the twentieth century's standard scholarly crib, and it still underpins the freely readable Odyssey on Perseus, where generations of students meet Homer line by line.

peers.name: Butler
peers.atlasBlurb: Samuel Butler wanted an Odyssey that reads like a novel, and in 1900 he produced the plainest English version yet: 'Tell me, O Muse, of that ingenious hero.' In his preface he prints Butcher & Lang's stately rendering beside his own precisely to show how far he has departed. The translation was written to accompany The Authoress of the Odyssey (1897), his cheerfully heretical case that a young Sicilian woman composed the poem. Free on Project Gutenberg in text and audio, it became — and remains — one of the easiest Odysseys to find and read online.

peers.name: Butcher & Lang
peers.atlasBlurb: The Victorian standard: Butcher and Lang's 1879 prose Odyssey, cast in deliberately archaic, King James-flavored English — "Tell me, Muse, of that man, so ready at need." For a generation of English readers this was simply how Homer sounded, and its authority is best measured by its critics: when Samuel Butler published his plain-prose Odyssey in 1900, he reprinted Butcher and Lang's opening in his own preface expressly so readers could see "how far I have departed from strict construe."

peers.name: Pope
peers.atlasBlurb: Pope's Odyssey was a workshop production behind a single glittering style: William Broome englished eight books (2, 6, 8, 11, 12, 16, 18, 23) and compiled the notes, Elijah Fenton four (1, 4, 19, 20), and Pope the remaining twelve — the whole polished into uniform heroic couplets so successfully that Broome's imitation of his master nearly defies identification. Issued by Bernard Lintot in five folio volumes under royal privilege (1725–26), it fixed the sound of Homer for the English eighteenth century.

peers.name: Cowper
peers.atlasBlurb: Cowper conceived his Homer as the antidote to Pope: blank verse instead of rhyme, closeness instead of couplet glitter. Joseph Johnson published the two quarto volumes in 1791, the second carrying the Odyssey together with the Battle of the Frogs and Mice. The proem sets the tone at once — plain, exact, and deliberately unmusical about its hero's cleverness: "Muse make the man thy theme, for shrewdness famed / And genius versatile." Every later blank-verse Odyssey in this catalog works in the space Cowper opened.

peers.name: Chapman
peers.atlasBlurb: The first complete Odyssey in English, capping the labor that made Chapman "Homeri Metaphrastes" — Homer's Englisher. Where his Iliads rolls in long fourteeners, the Odysses moves in rhymed iambic pentameter, freely expanded so that Odysseus becomes a pilgrim of wisdom rather than a plain wanderer. Gathered into The Whole Works of Homer (1616), the first complete English Homer, it stood alone for generations — and one October night in 1816 it kept John Keats and Cowden Clarke up till dawn, yielding the sonnet "On First Looking into Chapman's Homer" by morning.

peers.name: Johnston
peers.atlasBlurb: Ian Johnston's blank-verse Odyssey first appeared online in 2002, in print with Richer Resources in 2006, and as a Naxos audiobook in 2007. In January 2024 Johnston released the translation into the public domain, free to download, distribute, edit, and adapt. Plain-spoken and paced for reading aloud, the text remains available through web archives after the original site went dark.

peers.name: Bryant
peers.atlasBlurb: America's senior poet published his blank-verse Odyssey in Boston in 1871, in his late seventies. The verse is grave, plain, and unhurried — his hero is "Ulysses, the sagacious," the Latin names kept for readers raised on them — and it stands as the major American poetic Odyssey of the nineteenth century. An Osgood printing of 1873, two years after the 1871 copyright, shows the version already in re-issue; the University of Toronto scan of that printing is clean and complete.

peers.name: Palmer
peers.atlasBlurb: 'Speak to me, Muse, of the adventurous man' — Harvard philosophy professor George Herbert Palmer opened one of the most widely read American prose Odysseys. He published Books I–XII in 1884 and the complete poem in 1891, in supple, faintly rhythmic prose that reads well aloud. Houghton Mifflin kept it before generations of students: it was still being reissued in the Riverside Literature Series in the 1920s.

peers.name: Morris
peers.atlasBlurb: William Morris turned Homer into a northern romance: 'Tell me, O Muse, of the Shifty, the man who wandered afar.' The designer-poet cast the whole Odyssey in long rhymed couplets thick with deliberately archaic, saga-flavoured diction — 'Holy Burg', 'menfolk', 'fellow-farers'. Reviewing it in 1887, Oscar Wilde called it 'a true work of art, a rendering not merely of language into language, but of poetry into poetry.'

peers.name: Worsley
peers.atlasBlurb: Worsley remade the Odyssey in the nine-line stanza of Spenser's Faerie Queene, arguing in his preface that if rhyme is to be used at all, the metre of the Faerie Queene "is entitled to a trial" — and pushing back, politely but firmly, against Matthew Arnold, who had treated translating Homer in Spenserians as "not worth arguing." The result is the great stanzaic Odyssey in English: romance-colored, musical, complete in two volumes (1861–62), and still being reprinted by Blackwood in 1877.

records.name: Polylas

atlas.blurb: The Odyssey brought home into Modern Greek. Polylas — Corfu man of letters from Solomos's circle and a partisan of the demotic tongue — recast Homer in the unrhymed fifteen-syllable iambic line of Greek folk song, in an early demotic still trailing archaic remnants. Published in Athens from 1875 by the press of the Efimeris ton Syzitiseon, it opened the modern line of demotic Homers that runs through Eftaliotis to Kazantzakis–Kakridis.

peers.name: Pindemonte
peers.atlasBlurb: Ippolito Pindemonte spent his last years turning the Odyssey into Italian blank verse, published at Verona in 1822. Its opening — 'Musa, quell'uom di moltiforme ingegno / dimmi' — became one of the most famous incipits in Italian literature, and the translation ran through countless editions and reprints to reign as the Italian Odyssey for over a century. Its musical hendecasyllables even taught Brazil's Odorico Mendes how to build Homeric compound epithets.
